title: Clean on the outside (Luke 11:37–54)
hook: he eats with Pharisees and challenges religion that's all surface

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamp of the eye, and a single, generous eye that fills the whole body with light. Your line was keep the light in. Did you look at someone again, on purpose? Day five hundred forty-six.

A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner. That alone is worth noticing: Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once. And the Pharisees in this scene care about holiness at the table itself: washing, tithing, cups and dishes. So when the guest sits straight down without washing, the host is startled. The King James Bible says he "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner." And Jesus, at someone else's table, answers the look on his face.

"Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness." Ravening means grabbing, greed. It's a sharp thing to say at dinner, and Luke doesn't soften it. Then a question that turns it into a riddle: "did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?" God made the cup's inside as well as its outside. You can't polish one and ignore the other. His answer to how is surprising: give alms from what's within, and everything is clean. Generosity cleans the inside of the cup. Then he names their careful tithing, a tenth of even mint and rue from the herb garden, and says they pass over justice and the love of God. But listen to how the sentence ends: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." He doesn't throw out the small faithful habits. He says do both. This is the language of Israel's own prophets, speaking to their own people. Micah asked what the Lord requires, and answered: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. It's an argument inside a family, and any church can hear it about itself. And so a week on the road closes. Wisdom given to little ones. A Samaritan who stopped. Martha and Mary. A short prayer. A friend knocking at midnight. A lamp in the eye. And now a cup that needs washing on both sides.
screen: `DO BOTH: THE SMALL AND THE GREAT.`
then, large: `NOT TO LEAVE THE OTHER UNDONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean something inside, not just outside. If there's a cup or a bowl near you, pick it up and look into it. If not, picture one. Then turn your attention inward. What's sitting inside you that nobody else can see? A grudge, a little greed, a story you tell yourself about someone. Don't scrub at it. Just name it honestly. Then think of one generous thing you could give today, from the inside out: time, money, a kind word you've been holding back. If you pray, you can offer that inside place to God as it is. If you don't, simply let it be named. The bell holds the time.
Alms. Jesus's answer to how the inside of the cup gets clean: give from what's within to the poor, and everything is made clean.
Your line: the inside too. Today, when you tidy up to be seen by someone, do one quiet, generous thing nobody will see. Day five hundred forty-six, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Some Christians pair outward practices, like grace before meals, tithing or fasting, with an inward examination of conscience, and the season of Lent joins fasting with prayer and almsgiving, the giving this passage names.

fork.reveal: the Pharisee "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner," and Jesus answers with the cup: the inside matters too.

original.note: Greek: from within, the inside. the part of the cup, and of a person, that Jesus says God also made.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was against religious rules.
what it means: he says the outward habits should be done, and the inside cleaned too, through justice, love of God and generosity.
what a scholar hears: he speaks as Israel's prophets did, from inside the tradition, as a guest at a Pharisee's table, not from outside it.

notes: Pharisees described as a devoted movement seeking holiness in daily life (meals, purity). Framed to avoid making them a foil; please check tone.
Luke 11:41 ('give alms of such things as ye have') is ambiguous in Greek ('the things within'); script paraphrases as 'give alms from what's within'. Confirm.
Claim that Jewish teachers have made the same inward/outward point since: stated generally. Confirm framing.
